headline: Ohio Mayors Alliance pushes bipartisan Core Cities Transformation Fund — 31 cities seek ~$100M/year from state sales-tax growth for site-readiness and redevelopment
paragraphs: A bipartisan group of 31 Ohio mayors released a four-part policy agenda September 4, 2026, addressed to the incoming governor and new state legislature. The headline item is the Ohio Core Cities Transformation Fund: a proposal to set aside 20 percent of annual sales and use tax revenue growth — projected at roughly $100 million per year — for competitive planning grants, implementation grants, and zero-interest loans to help cities prepare sites, modernize infrastructure, leverage private investment, and complete catalytic redevelopment projects. Lima Mayor Sharetta Smith put the top-line figure at $100 million per year; Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz stressed the mechanism's political design: 'This does not raise a tax. This doesn't redirect a penny.' The fund draws only from year-over-year revenue growth, leaving existing budget commitments untouched.

Coverage of the Ohio Mayors Alliance recommendations ran simultaneously September 4 in The Toledo Blade, the Statehouse News Bureau, Ideastream Public Media, WOSU, WVXU, and WYSO — a statewide echo reflecting the breadth of the 31-city coalition, which spans Republican- and Democrat-led cities. Kapszukiewicz framed the fund as a project that 'benefits everyone.' The Alliance's full agenda includes three additional policy asks beyond the transformation fund, which were not detailed in available reporting as of this brief.
why_it_matters: Toledo is actively competing for site-readiness dollars across multiple fronts — Vibrancy Initiative grants, RAISE-funded infrastructure, brownfield remediation, and Vantage/data-center-related land preparation. A state fund providing competitive grants and zero-interest loans for exactly those activities would directly accelerate the pipeline Toledo's economic development offices are already working. The bipartisan framing — 31 cities, Republican and Democratic mayors alike — gives the proposal more legislative viability than a city-only ask typically carries in Columbus. Whether the incoming governor and new legislature adopt the fund in 2027 is the question to watch.
